solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In communist land, conservative almost a sitting duck, perhaps

parts.note: Cuba is a communist state

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Tory in Cuba is a vulnerable target, a sitting duck in hostile territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sitting duck' looks like an easy target, but here it is a duck sitting on eggs; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A brooding duck keeps its eggs warm until they hatch, which is exactly what this device does artificially.

clue.text: One article put in bag, not the last for boy

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: put in says the article goes inside the trimmed bag word
not the last means the final letter of the bag word is dropped

parts.note: to bag or sack, as a noun, a sack is a bag
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An instruction for packing: one item goes into a bag, but not the last one.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac is a male given name, so a boy may be called by it.

clue.text: Smoke rings in rock

indicators.note: in places the ring letters inside the rock word

parts.note: chert is a hard flinty sedimentary rock
two rings are two O shapes

explanation.surface: Smoke rings drifting among rocks, or smoke ringing a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar with both ends cut square, something one smokes.

clue.text: Secures trophy, pocketing pounds? I can't see it

indicators.note: pocketing means the securing word takes the pounds letter inside it

parts.note: to secure something is to bind it
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from Latin libra
a pot is slang for a sporting trophy or cup

explanation.surface: Someone ties down a trophy full of cash, then confesses to missing something.
explanation.definitionFit: A blind spot is an area where one's vision, or understanding, fails, so it is what one cannot see.

clue.text: The race of Man?

parts.note: the Isle of Man's emblem, the triskelion, is three running legs; and a sports-day race ties partners' legs together, three to a pair

explanation.surface: A grand question about the human race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea whose flag shows three legs; 'race' is a running race, not humanity.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manx emblem has three legs, and the sports-day race where partners tie two legs together carries the same name.

clue.text: Top of hill, not the first in series

indicators.note: not the first means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: the brow of a hill is its summit

explanation.surface: Looking along a range of hilltops, ignoring the nearest one.
explanation.definitionFit: A row is a line of things one after another, as a series is.

clue.text: Holding this to drink in study?

definitions.meaning: one holds a ... to one's lips to drink, read literally
British slang for cramming for an exam

explanation.surface: Someone holding a drink while studying, sipping as they read.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is literal and is completed by the answer itself, a mug raised; the second is the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Mugging up is informal British for swotting, studying intensively at short notice.

clue.text: Old Mexican's refusal in the morning to get up

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: nay is an old word for no
a.m. marks hours in the morning

explanation.surface: An old Mexican refuses to get out of bed in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maya were the pre-Columbian civilisation of southern Mexico and Central America.

clue.text: Guinea's principal parrots are beauties

indicators.note: the principal letter of a word is its first one

parts.note: lories are small brightly coloured parrots

explanation.surface: The finest parrots of Guinea are lovely birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Glories are things of great beauty or splendour, like the glories of nature.

clue.text: Convert polyester into a new form

indicators.note: putting into a new form rearranges the letters of the fabric word

explanation.surface: Instructions to recycle polyester fabric into something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convert' looks like a verb with 'polyester' its object, but it is a noun, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A proselyte is a person who has changed religion or belief, a convert.

clue.text: Drawing room?

parts.note: not a formal parlour but a room where drawing and painting are done

explanation.walkthrough: A drawing room is a sitting room, but read literally it is a room for drawing, an artist's studio.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop or studio.

clue.text: In hearing, judiciously consider African country excellent

indicators.note: in hearing says the weighing word is to be taken as it is spoken

parts.note: to weigh something is to consider it carefully
Togo is a country in West Africa

explanation.surface: At a hearing, someone weighs up an African country's case carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Way to go!' is an exclamation of praise for a job well done, as is 'excellent!'.

clue.text: Constant, endless mob in Circle Line

parts.note: c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a horde is a crowd or mob

explanation.surface: A steady crowd packed onto London's Circle Line underground trains.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground line, but here it is a line in a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a chord is a straight line joining two points on a circle's circumference.

clue.text: Dear old husband maybe mulling things over

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, such as a husband
pensive means deep in thought

explanation.surface: An affectionate address to a former husband who is lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' looks like a form of address to the husband but means costly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dear in the sense of high-priced: something costly or pricey.

clue.text: Writers on island puffed endlessly, entitled to payment

parts.note: pens are writing implements
Iona is an island of the Inner Hebrides, off western Scotland

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: blew means puffed out air

explanation.surface: Authors on a Scottish island, out of breath, claim their due.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is pensionable has reached the age or service qualifying them for a retirement income.

clue.text: Become hard, as quiz questions are?

definitions.meaning: jelly or concrete ... when it solidifies
quiz questions are ... by a quizmaster

explanation.surface: Quiz questions that are getting harder.
explanation.definitionFit: To set is to solidify; and questions written for a quiz are said to be set.

clue.text: Drop brainless type at end of match that may precede Ashes

parts.note: to sack someone is to drop them from a team or job
a clot is British slang for a stupid person

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A dim cricketer is dropped after a match ahead of the Ashes series.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England-Australia cricket series; here it is ashes of repentance, in the phrase 'sackcloth and ashes'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom of penitence is 'sackcloth and ashes', so the coarse cloth comes first in the phrase.

clue.text: Improbable promise of high tea?

parts.note: an unlikely promise, and literally a pie served high up as a meal in the air

explanation.walkthrough: High tea is an early evening meal in Britain; here 'high' suggests a meal in the sky, as on a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a hope or promise that is unrealistic and unlikely ever to be fulfilled.

clue.text: Scholar may disappear into thin air: so?

indicators.note: the answer's letters vanish into the clue's phrase, rearranged, so the phrase is their anagram

explanation.surface: An academic might vanish without trace, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May disappear into' is an unusual anagram signal: the answer's letters reappear jumbled in THIN AIR SO.
explanation.definitionFit: A historian is an expert who studies and writes about the past, a kind of scholar.

clue.text: Seriously engage old aeroplane with no luggage

parts.note: the de Havilland Comet was the first commercial jet airliner
no as a score is nil, or O
grips are travelling bags

explanation.surface: Boarding a vintage aircraft without any bags.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to grips with a problem is to tackle it in earnest.

clue.text: Result once of the functioning of the Dartmoor sewers

definitions.text: Result once of the functioning of the Dartmoor sewers

parts.words: Result once of the functioning of the Dartmoor sewers
parts.note: sewers are people who sew, not drains: inmates of Dartmoor prison once sewed postal sacks

explanation.walkthrough: Dartmoor is a prison in Devon; 'sewers' are those who sew. Sewing mailbags was once standard prison labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Convicts were set to stitching the canvas sacks the Post Office used for letters.

clue.text: His poetry no-go, his prose uneven?

indicators.note: uneven picks the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a writer's verse and his patchy prose.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two wordplays: odd letters of 'prose', and POETRY without TRY (go). The second also hints at the author, so it stands as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan Poe wrote both poetry and prose; removing an attempt from his poetry leaves his name.

clue.text: Support the mad OT character

parts.note: a prop is a support

indicators.note: mad suggests the letters of the little word are jumbled

explanation.surface: Backing the crazy Old Testament figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament contains many prophets, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah, who spoke for God.

clue.text: Paid for part of education, covered by two features of card

indicators.note: covered by means the education letters sit inside the card features

parts.note: credit cards have a chip and a PIN

explanation.surface: Paying part of school fees by card.
explanation.definitionFit: To chip in is to contribute a share of a cost.

clue.text: Head needs name plate

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: A headstone needs a nameplate.
explanation.definitionFit: A paten is the plate holding the bread at the Eucharist.

clue.text: Gas is round precinct

parts.note: a round shape is an O
a precinct is a district or zone

explanation.surface: A gas is spreading around the district.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozone is a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule, a gas.

clue.text: Like an aristocrat, could one say, ahead of his time?

definitions.text: Like an aristocrat, could one say
definitions.meaning: a jokey adjective, earl-y, as if 'like an earl'

explanation.surface: A nobleman with visionary ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a made-up adjective from earl plus -y; 'could one say' admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Early means before the usual or appointed hour, ahead of time.

clue.text: Like the M25, said to have got built in at intervals

indicators.note: to have got something in is to contain it, so the spoken word takes the picked letters inside
in completes the containment, the picked letters going into the spoken word

parts.note: oral means spoken

indicators.note: at intervals picks every other letter, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Rumour has it the M25 motorway was built bit by bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The M25 is the motorway that rings London. 'At intervals' gives BIT from 'built', which goes into ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The M25 is London's orbital motorway, one that circles the city.

clue.text: Tragic character (not Romeo!) that's slowly trampled by the herd

definitions.text: that's slowly trampled by the herd

indicators.note: not removes the letter that follows from the character's name

parts.note: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic hero
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean figure, not Romeo, stamped on by a stampeding crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition echoes Gray's Elegy: 'The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a meadow or pasture where cattle graze.

clue.text: Rabbit is more carefree

definitions.meaning: to rabbit is British slang for chattering on
... as the comparative of blithe means more carefree

explanation.surface: A rabbit is more cheerful than most.
explanation.definitionFit: Blither (short i) is to babble; blither (long i) is happier, more lighthearted.

clue.text: One appearing in Wagner partial to Bayreuth agent

indicators.note: partial to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An agent at the Bayreuth festival is fond of Wagner.
explanation.walkthrough: Bayreuth is the German town whose festival is devoted to Wagner's operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Hagen is the villain of Götterdämmerung, the last opera in Wagner's Ring cycle.

clue.text: From a foreign capital, your biscuit

parts.note: Berne is the capital of Switzerland
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Your biscuit has come from a city abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: An Abernethy is a hard Scottish biscuit flavoured with caraway.
